newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi authorities say questioning five plotters.
newsitem.headline: Burundi authorities say questioning five plotters.

text.p: Burundian authorities said on Thursday they were interrogating five people, including a former Rwandan soldier, closely linked to a former president after foiling a plot to assassinate military ruler Pierre Buyoya.
Buyoya's spokesman, Jean-Luc Ndizeye, said there was so far no evidence to link the plot to former president Jean-Baptiste Bagaza, a leading Tutsi critic of Buyoya.
He said the assassination plot was in no way connected to three mine blasts in the capital on Wednesday night that killed four people including a Burundian doctor and badly wounded two.
But he dismissed the idea that Hutu rebels were behind the blasts, saying they did not have the capacity for such attacks.

"Some of these (arrested) people have close links with Bagaza but we cannot say he is also involved. There is no evidence so far to suggest his involvement," Ndizeye told Reuters by telephone from the Burundi capital Bujumbura.
He said a former Rwandan soldier involved in the plot, which authorities said they foiled on Wednesday when they arrested the five, was a deserter from Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army.
He said Buyoya, a retired Tutsi major who seized power last July in a coup by the Tutsi-dominated Burundian army, was unshaken and was continuing his normal schedule of work.
"The plot was close to coming to fruition and everything had been put in place. Had they not been apprehended they could have carried out the plot within hours, not days," Ndizeye said.
Interior Minister Lieutenant-Colonel Epitace Bayaganakandi announced the plot on Wednesday and called for calm. The other four arrested were two Burundian army officers and two civilians.

The reported plot was the first against Buyoya since he took power from a Hutu civilian president. Two main groups oppose his rule -- Hutu rebels and Tutsi radicals under Bagaza who have strong links in the army.
Regional states imposed sanctions on Burundi shortly after the coup demanding unconditional talks between the government and rebels led by Hutu guerrilla leader Leonard Nyangoma.
More than 150,000 people have died in Burundi in massacres and civil war since the first freely elected Hutu president, Melchior Ndadaye, was murdered by Tutsi troops in October 1993.
Bagaza has been under house arrest since January. Police said they raided his house and found guns, grenades and subversive papers. Buyoya ousted Bagaza in 1987.
Since October, 200,000 Tutsis and Hutus have been put by the army in "regroupment camps", officially to protect them from Hutu rebels. U.N. human rights monitors say Hutus are forced into the camps.
The secretary-general of the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party has said they were the equivalent of concentration camps and was arrested last month and held in solitary confinement for a week.
